narrative:
Your application was denied because the prediction estimated a 61.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—meaning failure was judged more likely than passing. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it was strong enough to drive the denial.

The most influential factor was your third-year class-rank decile: you were in the 2nd decile, while accepted students averaged about 5.79. That comparatively low rank pushed the prediction toward failure. The second most influential factor was your first-year class-rank decile: you were in the 3rd decile versus an accepted average of about 6.00, which also pushed toward failure. The third most important factor was your family-income bracket. Being upper-middle income was common among accepted students and worked slightly in your favor, toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the academic-rank signals.

Your LSAT score of 31 and undergraduate GPA of 2.10 are also below the accepted averages shown (37.18 and 3.23), so they reinforce the concern even though they were not the top three drivers.

Next, ask admissions for feedback, speak with an advisor about whether reapplying is realistic, and build a clear improvement plan. Focus on raising your academic record in advanced coursework, preparing for and possibly retaking the LSAT, and documenting sustained improvement before reapplying or applying to programs with more holistic review.
